meta.sourceDocument: Cambridge International AS & A Level Physics 9702 syllabus for 2025, 2026 and 2027 (version 1, September 2022)
meta.validFor: Exams in 2025, 2026 and 2027 (June and November series; March series in India)

sections.title: Physical quantities and units
sections.summary: Physical quantities and units. Subsections: Physical quantities; SI units; Errors and uncertainties; Scalars and vectors.

topics.title: Physical quantities
outcomes: Understand that every physical quantity has a numerical magnitude and a unit.
Make reasonable estimates of physical quantities included in the syllabus.

topics.title: SI units
outcomes: Recall the SI base quantities and their units: mass (kg), length (m), time (s), current (A), temperature (K).
Express derived units as products or quotients of SI base units and use the derived units for the quantities in the syllabus.
Use SI base units to check the homogeneity of physical equations.
Recall and use the prefixes pico, nano, micro, milli, centi, deci, kilo, mega, giga and tera with their symbols.

topics.title: Errors and uncertainties
outcomes: Understand and explain the effects of systematic errors (including zero errors) and random errors in measurements.
Understand the difference between precision and accuracy.
Assess the uncertainty in a derived quantity by simple addition of absolute or percentage uncertainties.

topics.title: Scalars and vectors
outcomes: Understand the difference between scalar and vector quantities and give examples of each from the syllabus.
Add and subtract coplanar vectors.
Represent a vector as two perpendicular components.

sections.title: Kinematics
sections.summary: Kinematics. Subsections: Equations of motion.

topics.title: Equations of motion
outcomes: Define and use distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration.
Use graphical methods to represent distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration.
Determine displacement from the area under a velocity–time graph.
Determine velocity from the gradient of a displacement–time graph.
Determine acceleration from the gradient of a velocity–time graph.
Derive, from the definitions of velocity and acceleration, the equations for uniformly accelerated motion in a straight line.
Solve problems using the equations for uniformly accelerated motion in a straight line, including bodies falling in a uniform gravitational field without air resistance.
Describe an experiment to determine the acceleration of free fall using a falling object.
Describe and explain motion with uniform velocity in one direction and uniform acceleration in a perpendicular direction.

sections.title: Dynamics
sections.summary: Dynamics. Subsections: Momentum and Newton's laws of motion; Non-uniform motion; Linear momentum and its conservation.

topics.title: Momentum and Newton's laws of motion
outcomes: Understand that mass is the property of an object that resists change in motion.
Recall F = ma and solve problems with it, understanding that acceleration and resultant force are always in the same direction.
Define and use linear momentum as the product of mass and velocity.
Define and use force as the rate of change of momentum.
State and apply each of Newton's laws of motion.
Describe and use weight as the effect of a gravitational field on a mass, and recall that weight equals mass times the acceleration of free fall.

topics.title: Non-uniform motion
outcomes: Show a qualitative understanding of frictional forces and viscous/drag forces including air resistance (coefficients of friction and viscosity are not required; a simple model of drag increasing with speed is sufficient).
Describe and explain qualitatively the motion of objects in a uniform gravitational field with air resistance.
Understand that an object moving against a resistive force may reach a terminal (constant) velocity.

topics.title: Linear momentum and its conservation
outcomes: State the principle of conservation of momentum.
Apply conservation of momentum to solve simple problems, including elastic and inelastic interactions in one and two dimensions (the coefficient of restitution is not required).
Recall that in an elastic collision total kinetic energy is conserved and the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation.
Understand that the momentum of a system is always conserved in interactions, although some kinetic energy may change.

sections.title: Forces, density and pressure
sections.summary: Forces, density and pressure. Subsections: Turning effects of forces; Equilibrium of forces; Density and pressure.

topics.title: Turning effects of forces
outcomes: Understand that the weight of an object may be taken as acting at a single point, its centre of gravity.
Define and apply the moment of a force.
Understand that a couple is a pair of forces that produces rotation only.
Define and apply the torque of a couple.

topics.title: Equilibrium of forces
outcomes: State and apply the principle of moments.
Understand that a system with no resultant force and no resultant torque is in equilibrium.
Use a vector triangle to represent coplanar forces in equilibrium.

topics.title: Density and pressure
outcomes: Define and use density.
Define and use pressure.
Derive the hydrostatic pressure equation Δp = ρgΔh from the definitions of pressure and density.
Use Δp = ρgΔh.
Understand that the upthrust on an object in a fluid is due to a difference in hydrostatic pressure.
Calculate upthrust using F = ρgV (Archimedes' principle).

sections.title: Work, energy and power
sections.summary: Work, energy and power. Subsections: Energy conservation; Gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy.

topics.title: Energy conservation
outcomes: Understand work, and recall and use work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force.
Recall and apply the principle of conservation of energy.
Recall and understand that efficiency is the ratio of useful energy output to total energy input.
Use efficiency to solve problems.
Define power as work done per unit time.
Solve problems using P = W/t.
Derive P = Fv and use it to solve problems.

topics.title: Gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy
outcomes: Derive, using W = Fs, ΔEP = mgΔh for gravitational potential energy changes in a uniform gravitational field.
Recall and use ΔEP = mgΔh.
Derive, using the equations of motion, the kinetic energy formula EK = ½mv².
Recall and use EK = ½mv².

sections.title: Deformation of solids
sections.summary: Deformation of solids. Subsections: Stress and strain; Elastic and plastic behaviour.

topics.title: Stress and strain
outcomes: Understand that deformation is caused by tensile or compressive forces (one dimension only).
Understand and use the terms load, extension, compression and limit of proportionality.
Recall and use Hooke's law.
Recall and use the spring constant k = F/x.
Define and use stress, strain and the Young modulus.
Describe an experiment to determine the Young modulus of a metal in the form of a wire.

topics.title: Elastic and plastic behaviour
outcomes: Understand and use the terms elastic deformation, plastic deformation and elastic limit.
Understand that the area under a force–extension graph represents the work done.
Determine the elastic potential energy of a material deformed within its limit of proportionality from the area under the force–extension graph.
Recall and use EP = ½Fx = ½kx² for a material deformed within its limit of proportionality.

sections.title: Waves
sections.summary: Waves. Subsections: Progressive waves; Transverse and longitudinal waves; Doppler effect for sound waves; Electromagnetic spectrum; Polarisation.

topics.title: Progressive waves
outcomes: Describe wave motion as illustrated by vibrations in ropes, springs and ripple tanks.
Understand and use the terms displacement, amplitude, phase difference, period, frequency, wavelength and speed.
Understand how the time-base and y-gain of a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) are used to determine frequency and amplitude.
Derive the wave equation v = fλ from the definitions of speed, frequency and wavelength.
Recall and use v = fλ.
Understand that energy is transferred by a progressive wave.
Recall and use intensity = power/area and intensity ∝ amplitude² for a progressive wave.

topics.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves
outcomes: Compare transverse and longitudinal waves.
Analyse and interpret graphical representations of transverse and longitudinal waves.

topics.title: Doppler effect for sound waves
outcomes: Understand that when a sound source moves relative to a stationary observer the observed frequency differs from the source frequency (a stationary source with a moving observer is not required).
Use fo = fs·v/(v ± vs) for the observed frequency when a sound source moves relative to a stationary observer.

topics.title: Electromagnetic spectrum
outcomes: State that all electromagnetic waves are transverse and travel with the same speed c in free space.
Recall the approximate wavelength ranges in free space of the main regions of the electromagnetic spectrum, from radio waves to γ-rays.
Recall that wavelengths of 400–700 nm in free space are visible to the human eye.

topics.title: Polarisation
outcomes: Understand that polarisation is a phenomenon associated with transverse waves.
Recall and use Malus's law (I = I₀cos²θ) for the intensity of plane-polarised electromagnetic waves after one or more polarising filters (the effect of a filter on unpolarised waves is not required).

sections.title: Superposition
sections.summary: Superposition. Subsections: Stationary waves; Diffraction; Interference; The diffraction grating.

topics.title: Stationary waves
outcomes: Explain and use the principle of superposition.
Understand experiments that demonstrate stationary waves using microwaves, stretched strings and air columns (end corrections are assumed negligible and are not required).
Explain the formation of a stationary wave using a graphical method and identify nodes and antinodes.
Understand how wavelength can be found from the positions of nodes or antinodes of a stationary wave.

topics.title: Diffraction
outcomes: Explain the meaning of diffraction.
Understand experiments that demonstrate diffraction, including the qualitative effect of gap width relative to wavelength, e.g. water waves in a ripple tank.

topics.title: Interference
outcomes: Understand the terms interference and coherence.
Understand experiments that demonstrate two-source interference using water waves in a ripple tank, sound, light and microwaves.
Understand the conditions required for two-source interference fringes to be observed.
Recall and use λ = ax/D for double-slit interference using light.

topics.title: The diffraction grating
outcomes: Recall and use d sinθ = nλ.
Describe the use of a diffraction grating to determine the wavelength of light (the structure and use of the spectrometer are not included).

sections.title: Electricity
sections.summary: Electricity. Subsections: Electric current; Potential difference and power; Resistance and resistivity.

topics.title: Electric current
outcomes: Understand that an electric current is a flow of charge carriers.
Understand that the charge on charge carriers is quantised.
Recall and use Q = It.
Use I = Anvq for a current-carrying conductor, where n is the number density of charge carriers.

topics.title: Potential difference and power
outcomes: Define the potential difference across a component as the energy transferred per unit charge.
Recall and use V = W/Q.
Recall and use P = VI, P = I²R and P = V²/R.

topics.title: Resistance and resistivity
outcomes: Define resistance.
Recall and use V = IR.
Sketch the I–V characteristics of a metallic conductor at constant temperature, a semiconductor diode and a filament lamp.
Explain that the resistance of a filament lamp increases with current because its temperature rises.
State Ohm's law.
Recall and use R = ρL/A.
Understand that the resistance of a light-dependent resistor (LDR) decreases as light intensity increases.
Understand that the resistance of a thermistor decreases as temperature increases (a negative temperature coefficient is assumed).

sections.title: D.C. circuits
sections.summary: D.C. circuits. Subsections: Practical circuits; Kirchhoff's laws; Potential dividers.

topics.title: Practical circuits
outcomes: Recall and use the circuit symbols shown in section 6 of the syllabus.
Draw and interpret circuit diagrams containing those symbols.
Define and use the electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source as the energy transferred per unit charge in driving charge around a complete circuit.
Distinguish between e.m.f. and potential difference (p.d.) in terms of energy.
Understand the effect of the internal resistance of a source of e.m.f. on the terminal potential difference.

topics.title: Kirchhoff's laws
outcomes: Recall Kirchhoff's first law and understand that it follows from conservation of charge.
Recall Kirchhoff's second law and understand that it follows from conservation of energy.
Derive, using Kirchhoff's laws, the formula for the combined resistance of resistors in series.
Use the formula for the combined resistance of resistors in series.
Derive, using Kirchhoff's laws, the formula for the combined resistance of resistors in parallel.
Use the formula for the combined resistance of resistors in parallel.
Use Kirchhoff's laws to solve simple circuit problems.

topics.title: Potential dividers
outcomes: Understand the principle of a potential divider circuit.
Recall and use the principle of the potentiometer for comparing potential differences.
Understand the use of a galvanometer in null methods.
Explain the use of thermistors and light-dependent resistors in potential dividers to give a potential difference that depends on temperature and light intensity.

sections.title: Particle physics
sections.summary: Particle physics. Subsections: Atoms, nuclei and radiation; Fundamental particles.

topics.title: Atoms, nuclei and radiation
outcomes: Infer from the α-particle scattering experiment that the nucleus exists and is very small.
Describe a simple model of the nuclear atom with protons, neutrons and orbital electrons.
Distinguish between nucleon number and proton number.
Understand that isotopes are forms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
Understand and use the notation for nuclides showing nucleon number and proton number.
Understand that nucleon number and charge are conserved in nuclear processes.
Describe the composition, mass and charge of α-, β- and γ-radiations (both β⁻ electrons and β⁺ positrons are included).
Understand that an antiparticle has the same mass but opposite charge to its particle, and that a positron is the antiparticle of the electron.
State that (electron) antineutrinos are produced in β⁻ decay and (electron) neutrinos in β⁺ decay.
Understand that α-particles have discrete energies while β-particles have a continuous range of energies because (anti)neutrinos are emitted in β-decay.
Represent α- and β-decay by radioactive decay equations, e.g. uranium-238 decaying to thorium-234 with emission of an α-particle.
Use the unified atomic mass unit (u) as a unit of mass.

topics.title: Fundamental particles
outcomes: Understand that a quark is a fundamental particle and that there are six flavours: up, down, strange, charm, top and bottom.
Recall and use the charge of each flavour of quark and understand that its antiquark has the opposite charge (no other quark properties are required).
Recall that protons and neutrons are not fundamental particles and describe them in terms of their quark composition.
Understand that a hadron may be a baryon (three quarks) or a meson (one quark and one antiquark).
Describe the changes to quark composition that take place in β⁻ and β⁺ decay.
Recall that electrons and neutrinos are fundamental particles called leptons.

sections.title: Motion in a circle
sections.summary: Motion in a circle. Subsections: Kinematics of uniform circular motion; Centripetal acceleration.

topics.title: Kinematics of uniform circular motion
outcomes: Define the radian and express angular displacement in radians.
Understand and use angular speed.
Recall and use ω = 2π/T and v = rω.

topics.title: Centripetal acceleration
outcomes: Understand that a force of constant magnitude always perpendicular to the direction of motion causes centripetal acceleration.
Understand that centripetal acceleration causes circular motion with constant angular speed.
Recall and use a = rω² and a = v²/r.
Recall and use F = mrω² and F = mv²/r.

sections.title: Gravitational fields
sections.summary: Gravitational fields. Subsections: Gravitational field; Gravitational force between point masses; Gravitational field of a point mass; Gravitational potential.

topics.title: Gravitational field
outcomes: Understand that a gravitational field is a field of force and define gravitational field strength as force per unit mass.
Represent a gravitational field by field lines.

topics.title: Gravitational force between point masses
outcomes: Understand that for a point outside a uniform sphere the mass of the sphere may be treated as a point mass at its centre.
Recall and use Newton's law of gravitation, F = Gm₁m₂/r².
Analyse circular orbits in gravitational fields by relating the gravitational force to the centripetal acceleration it causes.
Understand that a geostationary satellite stays above the same point on the Earth's surface, with an orbital period of 24 hours, orbiting west to east directly above the Equator.

topics.title: Gravitational field of a point mass
outcomes: Derive g = GM/r² for the gravitational field strength of a point mass from Newton's law of gravitation and the definition of field strength.
Recall and use g = GM/r².
Understand why g is approximately constant for small changes in height near the Earth's surface.

topics.title: Gravitational potential
outcomes: Define gravitational potential at a point as the work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity to that point.
Use φ = −GM/r for the gravitational potential in the field of a point mass.
Understand how gravitational potential leads to the gravitational potential energy of two point masses and use EP = −GMm/r.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.summary: Temperature. Subsections: Thermal equilibrium; Temperature scales; Specific heat capacity and specific latent heat.

topics.title: Thermal equilibrium
outcomes: Understand that (thermal) energy is transferred from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature.
Understand that regions of equal temperature are in thermal equilibrium.

topics.title: Temperature scales
outcomes: Understand that any physical property that varies with temperature can be used to measure temperature, and give examples: density of a liquid, volume of a gas at constant pressure, resistance of a metal, e.m.f. of a thermocouple.
Understand that the thermodynamic temperature scale does not depend on the property of any particular substance.
Convert between kelvin and degrees Celsius, recalling T/K = θ/°C + 273.15.
Understand that the lowest possible temperature is zero kelvin (absolute zero) on the thermodynamic scale.

topics.title: Specific heat capacity and specific latent heat
outcomes: Define and use specific heat capacity.
Define and use specific latent heat, distinguishing latent heat of fusion from latent heat of vaporisation.

sections.title: Ideal gases
sections.summary: Ideal gases. Subsections: The mole; Equation of state; Kinetic theory of gases.

topics.title: The mole
outcomes: Understand that amount of substance is an SI base quantity with the base unit mol.
Use molar quantities, where one mole contains a number of particles equal to the Avogadro constant NA.

topics.title: Equation of state
outcomes: Understand that a gas obeying pV ∝ T (T thermodynamic temperature) is an ideal gas.
Recall and use pV = nRT (n = amount of substance) and pV = NkT (N = number of molecules).
Recall that the Boltzmann constant is k = R/NA.

topics.title: Kinetic theory of gases
outcomes: State the basic assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases.

Explain how molecular movement causes gas pressure and derive and use pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩, where ⟨c²⟩ is the mean-square speed (a one-dimensional collision model extended to three dimensions using ⅓⟨c²⟩ = ⟨cx²⟩ is sufficient).
Understand that the root-mean-square speed is the square root of the mean-square speed.
Compare pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩ with pV = NkT to deduce that the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule is (3/2)kT, and recall and use this.

sections.title: Thermodynamics
sections.summary: Thermodynamics. Subsections: Internal energy; The first law of thermodynamics.

topics.title: Internal energy
outcomes: Understand that internal energy is determined by the state of the system and is the sum of the random distribution of kinetic and potential energies of its molecules.
Relate a rise in temperature of an object to an increase in its internal energy.

topics.title: The first law of thermodynamics
outcomes: Recall and use W = pΔV for the work done when a gas changes volume at constant pressure, distinguishing work done by the gas from work done on the gas.
Recall and use the first law of thermodynamics ΔU = q + W in terms of the increase in internal energy, the energy transferred to the system by heating, and the work done on the system.

sections.title: Oscillations
sections.summary: Oscillations. Subsections: Simple harmonic oscillations; Energy in simple harmonic motion; Damped and forced oscillations, resonance.

topics.title: Simple harmonic oscillations
outcomes: Understand and use the terms displacement, amplitude, period, frequency, angular frequency and phase difference for oscillations, and express the period in terms of frequency and of angular frequency.
Understand that simple harmonic motion occurs when acceleration is proportional to displacement from a fixed point and in the opposite direction.
Use a = −ω²x and recall and use x = x₀ sin ωt as a solution.
Use v = v₀ cos ωt and v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²).
Analyse and interpret graphs of displacement, velocity and acceleration against time for simple harmonic motion.

topics.title: Energy in simple harmonic motion
outcomes: Describe the interchange between kinetic and potential energy during simple harmonic motion.
Recall and use E = ½mω²x₀² for the total energy of a system in simple harmonic motion.

topics.title: Damped and forced oscillations, resonance
outcomes: Understand that a resistive force acting on an oscillating system causes damping.
Understand and use the terms light, critical and heavy damping and sketch displacement–time graphs for each.
Understand that resonance is a maximum amplitude of oscillation, occurring when a system is forced to oscillate at its natural frequency.

sections.title: Electric fields
sections.summary: Electric fields. Subsections: Electric fields and field lines; Uniform electric fields; Electric force between point charges; Electric field of a point charge; Electric potential.

topics.title: Electric fields and field lines
outcomes: Understand that an electric field is a field of force and define electric field strength as force per unit positive charge.
Recall and use F = qE for the force on a charge in an electric field.
Represent an electric field by field lines.

topics.title: Uniform electric fields
outcomes: Recall and use E = ΔV/Δd for the uniform field between charged parallel plates.
Describe the effect of a uniform electric field on the motion of charged particles.

topics.title: Electric force between point charges
outcomes: Understand that for a point outside a spherical conductor the charge on the sphere may be treated as a point charge at its centre.
Recall and use Coulomb's law F = Q₁Q₂/(4πε₀r²) for the force between two point charges in free space.

topics.title: Electric field of a point charge
outcomes: Recall and use E = Q/(4πε₀r²) for the electric field strength of a point charge in free space.

topics.title: Electric potential
outcomes: Define electric potential at a point as the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small test charge from infinity to that point.
Recall and use the fact that the electric field at a point equals the negative of the potential gradient there.
Use V = Q/(4πε₀r) for the electric potential in the field of a point charge.
Understand how electric potential leads to the electric potential energy of two point charges and use EP = Qq/(4πε₀r).

sections.title: Capacitance
sections.summary: Capacitance. Subsections: Capacitors and capacitance; Energy stored in a capacitor; Discharging a capacitor.

topics.title: Capacitors and capacitance
outcomes: Define capacitance for isolated spherical conductors and parallel-plate capacitors.
Recall and use C = Q/V.
Derive, using C = Q/V, the formulae for combined capacitance in series and in parallel.
Use the formulae for capacitors in series and in parallel.

topics.title: Energy stored in a capacitor
outcomes: Determine the electric potential energy stored in a capacitor from the area under the potential–charge graph.
Recall and use W = ½QV = ½CV².

topics.title: Discharging a capacitor
outcomes: Analyse graphs of potential difference, charge and current against time for a capacitor discharging through a resistor.
Recall and use τ = RC for the time constant of a capacitor discharging through a resistor.
Use equations of the form x = x₀e^(−t/RC), where x may be current, charge or potential difference for a capacitor discharging through a resistor.

sections.title: Magnetic fields
sections.summary: Magnetic fields. Subsections: Concept of a magnetic field; Force on a current-carrying conductor; Force on a moving charge; Magnetic fields due to currents; Electromagnetic induction.

topics.title: Concept of a magnetic field
outcomes: Understand that a magnetic field is a field of force produced by moving charges or by permanent magnets.
Represent a magnetic field by field lines.

topics.title: Force on a current-carrying conductor
outcomes: Understand that a force may act on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
Recall and use F = BIL sinθ, with directions given by Fleming's left-hand rule.
Define magnetic flux density as the force per unit current per unit length on a wire at right angles to the field.

topics.title: Force on a moving charge
outcomes: Determine the direction of the force on a charge moving in a magnetic field.
Recall and use F = BQv sinθ.
Understand the origin of the Hall voltage and derive and use VH = BI/(ntq), where t is the thickness.
Understand the use of a Hall probe to measure magnetic flux density.
Describe the motion of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its motion.
Explain how electric and magnetic fields can be used for velocity selection.

topics.title: Magnetic fields due to currents
outcomes: Sketch the magnetic field patterns of a long straight wire, a flat circular coil and a long solenoid.
Understand that a ferrous core increases the magnetic field of a solenoid.
Explain the origin of the forces between current-carrying conductors and determine their directions.

topics.title: Electromagnetic induction
outcomes: Define magnetic flux as magnetic flux density times the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the field.
Recall and use Φ = BA.
Understand and use magnetic flux linkage.

Understand and explain experiments showing that a changing magnetic flux induces an e.m.f. in a circuit, that the induced e.m.f. acts to oppose the change producing it, and the factors affecting its magnitude.
Recall and use Faraday's and Lenz's laws of electromagnetic induction.

sections.title: Alternating currents
sections.summary: Alternating currents. Subsections: Characteristics of alternating currents; Rectification and smoothing.

topics.title: Characteristics of alternating currents
outcomes: Understand and use the terms period, frequency and peak value for an alternating current or voltage.
Use equations of the form x = x₀ sin ωt for a sinusoidally alternating current or voltage.
Recall and use the fact that the mean power in a resistive load is half the maximum power for a sinusoidal alternating current.
Distinguish between r.m.s. and peak values and recall and use Ir.m.s. = I₀/√2 and Vr.m.s. = V₀/√2 for a sinusoidal alternating current.

topics.title: Rectification and smoothing
outcomes: Distinguish graphically between half-wave and full-wave rectification.
Explain the use of a single diode for half-wave rectification of an alternating current.
Explain the use of four diodes (bridge rectifier) for full-wave rectification of an alternating current.
Analyse the effect of a single smoothing capacitor, including the effect of the capacitance and the load resistance.

sections.title: Quantum physics
sections.summary: Quantum physics. Subsections: Energy and momentum of a photon; Photoelectric effect; Wave-particle duality; Energy levels in atoms and line spectra.

topics.title: Energy and momentum of a photon
outcomes: Understand that electromagnetic radiation has a particulate nature.
Understand that a photon is a quantum of electromagnetic energy.
Recall and use E = hf.
Use the electronvolt (eV) as a unit of energy.
Understand that a photon has momentum p = E/c.

topics.title: Photoelectric effect
outcomes: Understand that photoelectrons may be emitted from a metal surface illuminated by electromagnetic radiation.
Understand and use the terms threshold frequency and threshold wavelength.
Explain photoelectric emission in terms of photon energy and work function energy.
Recall and use hf = Φ + ½mv²max.
Explain why the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is independent of intensity while the photoelectric current is proportional to intensity.

topics.title: Wave-particle duality
outcomes: Understand that the photoelectric effect is evidence for the particulate nature of electromagnetic radiation, while interference and diffraction are evidence for its wave nature.
Describe and interpret qualitatively the evidence from electron diffraction for the wave nature of particles.
Understand the de Broglie wavelength as the wavelength associated with a moving particle.
Recall and use λ = h/p.

topics.title: Energy levels in atoms and line spectra
outcomes: Understand that isolated atoms (e.g. atomic hydrogen) have discrete electron energy levels.
Understand the appearance and formation of emission and absorption line spectra.
Recall and use hf = E₁ − E₂.

sections.title: Nuclear physics
sections.summary: Nuclear physics. Subsections: Mass defect and nuclear binding energy; Radioactive decay.

topics.title: Mass defect and nuclear binding energy
outcomes: Understand the equivalence of energy and mass, E = mc², and recall and use it.
Represent simple nuclear reactions by nuclear equations, e.g. nitrogen-14 plus helium-4 giving oxygen-17 plus a proton.
Define and use the terms mass defect and binding energy.
Sketch the variation of binding energy per nucleon with nucleon number.
Explain what is meant by nuclear fusion and nuclear fission.
Explain the relevance of binding energy per nucleon to nuclear reactions, including fusion and fission.
Calculate the energy released in nuclear reactions using E = c²Δm.

topics.title: Radioactive decay
outcomes: Understand that fluctuations in count rate provide evidence for the random nature of radioactive decay.
Understand that radioactive decay is both spontaneous and random.
Define activity and decay constant, and recall and use A = λN.
Define half-life.
Use λ = 0.693/t½.
Understand the exponential nature of radioactive decay, and sketch and use x = x₀e^(−λt), where x may be activity, number of undecayed nuclei or received count rate.

sections.title: Medical physics
sections.summary: Medical physics. Subsections: Production and use of ultrasound; Production and use of X-rays; PET scanning.

topics.title: Production and use of ultrasound
outcomes: Understand that a piezoelectric crystal changes shape when a p.d. is applied across it and generates an e.m.f. when its shape changes.
Understand how ultrasound waves are generated and detected by a piezoelectric transducer.
Understand how reflection of ultrasound pulses at tissue boundaries gives diagnostic information about internal structures.
Define the specific acoustic impedance of a medium as Z = ρc, where c is the speed of sound in the medium.
Use IR/I₀ = (Z₁ − Z₂)²/(Z₁ + Z₂)² for the intensity reflection coefficient of a boundary between two media.
Recall and use I = I₀e^(−μx) for the attenuation of ultrasound in matter.

topics.title: Production and use of X-rays
outcomes: Explain that X-rays are produced by electron bombardment of a metal target, and calculate the minimum wavelength of X-rays produced from the accelerating p.d.
Understand the use of X-rays in imaging internal body structures, including the term contrast in X-ray imaging.
Recall and use I = I₀e^(−μx) for the attenuation of X-rays in matter.
Understand that computed tomography (CT) scanning builds a 3D image by combining X-ray images taken from different angles into 2D section images and repeating along an axis.

topics.title: PET scanning
outcomes: Understand that a tracer is a substance containing radioactive nuclei that is introduced into the body and absorbed by the tissue being studied.
Recall that a tracer decaying by β⁺ decay is used in positron emission tomography (PET scanning).
Understand that annihilation occurs when a particle interacts with its antiparticle, with mass–energy and momentum conserved.
Explain that in PET scanning, positrons from the tracer annihilate with electrons in the tissue, producing a pair of gamma-ray photons travelling in opposite directions.
Calculate the energy of the gamma-ray photons emitted in the annihilation of an electron–positron pair.
Understand that the gamma photons travel out of the body and are detected, and that an image of tracer concentration is created by processing their arrival times.

sections.title: Astronomy and cosmology
sections.summary: Astronomy and cosmology. Subsections: Standard candles; Stellar radii; Hubble's law and the Big Bang theory.

topics.title: Standard candles
outcomes: Understand luminosity as the total power of radiation emitted by a star.
Recall and use the inverse square law for radiant flux intensity, F = L/(4πd²).
Understand that an object of known luminosity is called a standard candle.
Understand the use of standard candles to determine distances to galaxies.

topics.title: Stellar radii
outcomes: Recall and use Wien's displacement law, λmax ∝ 1/T, to estimate the peak surface temperature of a star.
Use the Stefan–Boltzmann law L = 4πσr²T⁴.
Use Wien's displacement law and the Stefan–Boltzmann law to estimate the radius of a star.

topics.title: Hubble's law and the Big Bang theory
outcomes: Understand that lines in the emission and absorption spectra of distant objects show an increase in wavelength from their known values.
Use Δλ/λ ≈ Δf/f ≈ v/c for the redshift of electromagnetic radiation from a source moving relative to an observer.
Explain why redshift leads to the idea that the Universe is expanding.
Recall and use Hubble's law v ≈ H₀d and explain how this leads to the Big Bang theory (only SI units are required).
